aeschylus.author: Aeschylus

facts.claim: The battle of Salamis was fought in 480 BC, traditionally dated to late September.
When news reached the Greek fleet at Salamis that the Acropolis had fallen, some commanders panicked and voted to sail away to the Isthmus.
Themistocles sent the message when he was losing the council debate to the Peloponnesian commanders, who wanted to leave Salamis and fight at the Isthmus.
Sicinnus was a slave of Themistocles' household and the tutor of his children.
Themistocles sent him by boat to the Persian commanders with a message: Themistocles was on the king's side, and the Greeks were terrified and planning to flee.
The message said that if the Persians stopped the Greeks escaping, they would see them fighting among themselves.
Aeschylus, eight years later, also tells of a Greek who came to Xerxes saying the Greeks would slip away under cover of night.
The Persians believed it: that night they moved their ships to close the channels around Salamis and landed soldiers on the islet of Psyttaleia.
Aristides, Themistocles' old rival who had been ostracised from Athens, crossed from Aegina and brought word that the fleet was surrounded.
Afterwards Themistocles made Sicinnus a citizen of Thespiae and a rich man.
Modern historians read the message as a deliberate trap to force the battle into the narrow strait.
In the narrow strait the crowded Persian ships could not use their numbers; they struck each other with their bronze rams and broke their oars.
